## Introduction

Higher-education institutions have a direct interest in identifying students
at risk of dropping out early enough to intervene. This report works through
a supervised multi-class classification approach to that problem, using
Kaggle's [Playground Series S4E6](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/playground-series-s4e6)
dataset — a synthetic-augmented version of the UCI "Predict Students' Dropout
and Academic Success" dataset.

The task: given a student's demographics, socioeconomic background,
admission record, and first/second-semester curricular performance, predict
whether they will ultimately be classified as **Dropout**, **Enrolled**
(still active, outcome pending), or **Graduate**.

This writeup accompanies `notebooks/01_eda_and_modeling.ipynb`, which
contains the full exploratory and modeling code. Here we focus on
*why* each step was taken and what it reveals, rather than repeating every
line of code.

## Data

The dataset has one row per student and roughly three groups of features:

- **Demographics & background** — marital status, nationality, whether the
  student is displaced from their region, has educational special needs,
  is a debtor, etc.
- **Admission record** — application mode/order, course, previous
  qualification and its grade, admission grade.
- **Curricular performance** — units credited/enrolled/evaluated/approved
  and average grade, separately for the 1st and 2nd semester.
- **Macroeconomic context** — unemployment rate, inflation rate, and GDP at
  the time of enrollment.

### What "1st sem" / "2nd sem" actually cover, and why that's enough

Each semester field breaks down as follows:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `credited` | Units credited without an exam (transfer credit, exemptions, prior qualifications) |
| `enrolled` | Units the student registered for that semester |
| `evaluations` | Number of evaluation instances (exams/assessments) undergone |
| `approved` | Units passed |
| `grade` | Average grade across that semester's evaluated units |
| `without evaluations` | Units enrolled in but never evaluated — disengagement, distinct from being evaluated *and* failing |

"1st sem"/"2nd sem" here means the student's **first academic year** —
Portuguese degree programs typically run 3+ years, and the target
(Dropout/Enrolled/Graduate) is recorded at the end of the program's normal
duration, years later. Predicting a multi-year outcome from only the first
year's data is not a limitation of this dataset — it *is* the point.

This reflects a real, well-studied use case: **early-warning dropout
prediction**. An institution doesn't want to wait until year 3 to notice a
student is at risk — by then it's often too late to intervene financially,
academically, or administratively. The actionable question is: *using only
what's known from admission plus the first year, can at-risk students be
flagged early enough to actually help them?* That framing is also why this
project's strongest engineered features — `approval_rate_1st_sem`/
`approval_rate_2nd_sem` and `grade_trend` — matter so much: a student's
*trajectory* within that first year (improving vs. declining, engaged vs.
disengaging) is a meaningful early signal for what happens over the
following years, even though the model never observes those later years
directly. The SHAP results below confirm this empirically.

Most "categorical" fields arrive as integer codes (see the UCI documentation
for the legend) rather than as strings — a common data-cleaning trap, since
a naive pipeline might treat them as ordinal numeric features instead of
unordered categories. This project's preprocessing pipeline
(`src/academic_success/features.py`) explicitly one-hot encodes them instead.

```{python}
#| label: fig-class-balance
#| fig-cap: "Target class distribution across the 76,518-row training set."
from academic_success import config, data

train_df = data.load_train()
counts = train_df[config.TARGET_COL].value_counts().reindex(config.TARGET_CLASSES)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
bars = ax.bar(counts.index, counts.values, color=PALETTE[:3], width=0.6)
for bar, value in zip(bars, counts.values):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, value + 600, f"{value:,}\n({value / counts.sum():.0%})",
            ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=10)
ax.set_ylabel("Students")
ax.set_ylim(0, counts.max() * 1.22)
ax.set_title("Target class balance")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this matters
The classes are moderately imbalanced (~47% Graduate / 33% Dropout / 20%
Enrolled). This is *why* every model comparison in this report uses
macro-averaged F1 rather than raw accuracy — a model that leans on the
majority "Graduate" class would otherwise look deceptively good.
:::

## Feature Engineering

Beyond the raw columns, `src/academic_success/features.py` derives features
that summarize a student's trajectory across the two semesters rather than
treating each semester in isolation:

- `approval_rate_1st_sem` / `approval_rate_2nd_sem` — the fraction of
  enrolled units a student actually passed, per semester. Two students who
  both "enroll in 6 units" look identical on the raw columns, but one who
  passes all 6 and one who passes 1 are very different risk profiles — the
  approval *rate* captures that, the raw counts alone don't.
- `total_units_approved` / `total_units_enrolled` — cumulative load and
  success across both semesters, a coarser but more stable signal than
  either semester alone.
- `grade_trend` — the change in average grade from the 1st to the 2nd
  semester. A student improving over time is a different risk profile from
  one declining, even at the same average grade.
- `no_evaluation_ratio` — the fraction of a student's units that were never
  evaluated at all (as opposed to evaluated and failed). This is a
  disengagement signal distinct from academic failure.
- `max_parental_qualification` — the higher of the mother's and father's
  qualification codes. **Caveat, stated plainly rather than glossed over:**
  these codes are categorical labels, not a ranked scale, so taking their
  numeric max is a common but imperfect Kaggle proxy for "at least one
  highly-coded parental qualification" — not a genuine ordinal measurement.

All ratio features guard against division by zero explicitly (mapping `0/0`
and `x/0` to `0` rather than `NaN`/`inf`) — a small but easy-to-miss data
cleaning detail that would otherwise silently corrupt every downstream row
for students with zero enrolled units in a semester.

```{python}
#| label: fig-approval-rate-by-outcome
#| fig-cap: "1st-semester approval rate by eventual outcome — the gap between Dropout and Graduate is exactly the signal this engineered feature was designed to expose."
from academic_success.features import FeatureEngineer

X_preview = train_df[config.RAW_FEATURE_COLS]
y_preview = train_df[config.TARGET_COL]
engineered_preview = FeatureEngineer().fit_transform(X_preview)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
sns.boxplot(
    x=y_preview, y=engineered_preview["approval_rate_1st_sem"], hue=y_preview, legend=False,
    order=config.TARGET_CLASSES, palette=PALETTE[:3], ax=ax, width=0.5,
)
ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.set_ylabel("1st-sem approval rate")
ax.set_title("Approval rate cleanly separates the three outcomes")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Rare-category grouping.** Several categorical columns have a long tail of
near-unique codes — verified against the real training data, `Father's
occupation` has 56 distinct codes, 44 of them below 1% frequency. One-hot
encoding all of them would fragment the feature space into columns the
model barely ever sees, and risks an unseen rare code at inference time
being treated identically to *every other* unseen code by
`OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")`'s all-zero encoding — rather than
being recognised as "the same kind of rare code" the model saw examples of
in training. `RareCategoryGrouper` collapses any category below a frequency
threshold into a shared sentinel *before* one-hot encoding, learned from
training data only (no test-time leakage).

## Methodology

**Preprocessing.** Numeric features (raw + engineered) are median-imputed
then standardized; categorical (integer-coded, rare-grouped) features are
most-frequent-imputed then one-hot encoded, with unseen categories at
inference time mapped to an all-zero encoding rather than raising an error.

**Model selection.** Rather than assuming one model family is best, the
project sweeps eight: a linear baseline (regularized logistic regression),
bagged trees (Random Forest), two classic boosting variants (AdaBoost,
Gradient Boosting), and four modern gradient-boosting implementations
(HistGradientBoosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) — see
`src/academic_success/model.py`'s `MODEL_FACTORIES`.

**Class imbalance.** The target is moderately imbalanced (~47% Graduate,
33% Dropout, 20% Enrolled). ADASYN (Adaptive Synthetic Sampling) was
evaluated as a mitigation, generating synthetic minority-class examples
concentrated near the decision boundary. Implemented via an
`imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline` so resampling only ever touches the training
fold — never validation or test data, which would otherwise leak synthetic
points into the score.

**Ensembling.** A stacking ensemble (Random Forest + XGBoost + LightGBM +
CatBoost feeding a logistic regression meta-learner via
`sklearn.StackingClassifier`) was evaluated against the best single model,
on a held-out split rather than nested cross-validation — `Stacking
Classifier` already runs its own internal 5-fold CV to generate the
meta-learner's training data, so an *outer* 5-fold CV on top would mean 25
fits per base model instead of 5.

**Interpretability.** SHAP (`shap.TreeExplainer`) attributes individual
predictions to feature contributions for the final tree-based model,
validating (or challenging) the feature-engineering rationale above against
what the model actually learned.

**Validation.** All model comparisons use 5-fold cross-validation, reporting
both accuracy and macro-averaged F1 — macro-F1 matters here because the
three target classes are not evenly distributed, and a model that mostly
predicts the majority class would look deceptively good on raw accuracy
alone.

## Results

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where these numbers come from
The tables and charts below transcribe the actual output of
`notebooks/01_eda_and_modeling.ipynb` Sections 9–12 (run against the real
downloaded competition data). They're hard-coded here rather than
recomputed on every report render — re-running an 8-model x 5-fold sweep
plus a stacking ensemble just to render a report would take several
minutes for no new information.
:::

### Model sweep

Stratified 15,000-row subsample, 5-fold CV, for fast iteration (see
Section 9 of the notebook):

```{python}
#| label: fig-model-sweep
#| fig-cap: "Cross-validated macro-F1 across all 8 model families (15,000-row subsample)."
sweep_results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"model": "Gradient Boosting", "accuracy": 0.8247, "f1_macro": 0.7846},
    {"model": "HistGradientBoosting", "accuracy": 0.8230, "f1_macro": 0.7839},
    {"model": "Logistic Regression", "accuracy": 0.8229, "f1_macro": 0.7806},
    {"model": "LightGBM", "accuracy": 0.8197, "f1_macro": 0.7790},
    {"model": "CatBoost", "accuracy": 0.8198, "f1_macro": 0.7783},
    {"model": "Random Forest", "accuracy": 0.8191, "f1_macro": 0.7770},
    {"model": "XGBoost", "accuracy": 0.8146, "f1_macro": 0.7727},
    {"model": "AdaBoost", "accuracy": 0.8133, "f1_macro": 0.7692},
]).sort_values("f1_macro")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
bars = ax.barh(sweep_results["model"], sweep_results["f1_macro"], color=PALETTE[0])
bars[-1].set_color(PALETTE[3])  # highlight the winner
ax.set_xlim(0.76, 0.79)
ax.set_xlabel("CV macro F1")
ax.set_title("Model sweep — Gradient Boosting edges out the field")
for bar, value in zip(bars, sweep_results["f1_macro"]):
    ax.text(value + 0.0006, bar.get_y() + bar.get_height() / 2, f"{value:.4f}", va="center", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Full-data final model

The project's saved default (HistGradientBoosting, `models/model.joblib`)
trained with 5-fold CV on the *full* 76,518-row training set reaches
**0.8317 accuracy / 0.7949 macro-F1** — beating *every* model in the
15,000-row sweep above, including the one that nominally "won" it.

::: {.callout-important}
## Data volume beat model choice
More training data mattered more than which model family was used, at
least within the model families tried here. This is a common — and
easy-to-miss — result: it's tempting to spend effort tuning/switching
models when spending it on getting more (or better-utilized) data would
pay off more.
:::

### Class imbalance: does ADASYN help?

Evaluated on the sweep's best model (Gradient Boosting, same 15,000-row
subsample):

```{python}
#| label: fig-adasyn-comparison
#| fig-cap: "ADASYN oversampling slightly hurt macro-F1 on this dataset."
resample_results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"resample": "None", "f1_macro": 0.7846},
    {"resample": "ADASYN", "f1_macro": 0.7829},
])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
bars = ax.bar(resample_results["resample"], resample_results["f1_macro"], color=[PALETTE[0], PALETTE[3]], width=0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0.77, 0.79)
ax.set_ylabel("CV macro F1")
ax.set_title("Resampling comparison")
for bar, value in zip(bars, resample_results["f1_macro"]):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, value + 0.0008, f"{value:.4f}", ha="center", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Ensembling: does stacking help?

Held-out 20% split, same subsample:

```{python}
#| label: fig-stacking-comparison
#| fig-cap: "The stacking ensemble roughly ties the best single model, at far higher training cost."
stacking_results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"model": "Best single model\n(Gradient Boosting)", "f1_macro": 0.7772},
    {"model": "Stacking ensemble", "f1_macro": 0.7742},
])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
bars = ax.bar(stacking_results["model"], stacking_results["f1_macro"], color=[PALETTE[4], PALETTE[3]], width=0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0.76, 0.79)
ax.set_ylabel("Holdout macro F1")
ax.set_title("Stacking vs. single model")
for bar, value in zip(bars, stacking_results["f1_macro"]):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, value + 0.0008, f"{value:.4f}", ha="center", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Two negative results, reported honestly
Neither ADASYN nor stacking improved on the simpler alternative — ADASYN
made macro-F1 slightly *worse*, and stacking essentially tied the single
model while costing far more to train. That's exactly why the project's
saved default model stays a single HistGradientBoostingClassifier rather
than the fancier options; see the Discussion below for why.
:::

### Model interpretability (SHAP)

HistGradientBoosting final model, 500-row sample, mean absolute SHAP value
averaged across all 3 classes:

```{python}
#| label: fig-shap-top-features
#| fig-cap: "Top 10 features by mean |SHAP value| — the engineered trajectory features dominate."
shap_results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"feature": "approval_rate_2nd_sem", "mean_abs_shap": 0.674},
    {"feature": "total_units_approved", "mean_abs_shap": 0.253},
    {"feature": "approval_rate_1st_sem", "mean_abs_shap": 0.180},
    {"feature": "Tuition fees up to date", "mean_abs_shap": 0.146},
    {"feature": "2nd-sem grade", "mean_abs_shap": 0.140},
    {"feature": "2nd-sem evaluations", "mean_abs_shap": 0.125},
    {"feature": "1st-sem grade", "mean_abs_shap": 0.099},
    {"feature": "Scholarship holder", "mean_abs_shap": 0.092},
    {"feature": "1st-sem evaluations", "mean_abs_shap": 0.084},
    {"feature": "Age at enrollment", "mean_abs_shap": 0.074},
]).sort_values("mean_abs_shap")

is_engineered = shap_results["feature"].str.contains("approval_rate|total_units")
colors = [PALETTE[3] if e else PALETTE[0] for e in is_engineered]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.8))
bars = ax.barh(shap_results["feature"], shap_results["mean_abs_shap"], color=colors)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean |SHAP value|")
ax.set_title("Engineered features (orange) dominate the top 3")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Discussion

Pulling the Results section's findings together: the engineered trajectory
features aren't just theoretically motivated (as argued in Feature
Engineering) — SHAP confirms they're what the model actually leans on most,
with `approval_rate_2nd_sem` alone outweighing the next-ranked feature by
more than 2.5x. That closes the loop between *why* a feature was built and
*whether* the model agrees it matters.

The two negative results (ADASYN, stacking) are worth sitting with rather
than rationalizing away. Both are standard "try this, it should help"
techniques — and neither did, here. That's precisely why this project keeps
a single HistGradientBoostingClassifier as its saved default
(`models/model.joblib`) rather than reaching for the more sophisticated
options by default: added complexity earns its place only when it earns
its keep, and `scripts/train.py --stacking` / `--resample` stay available
for anyone who wants to re-check that conclusion on a different split or at
full data scale.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Limitations
- This dataset is a Kaggle Playground competition — a synthetic-augmented
  version of the original UCI data. Real-world deployment on a different
  institution's population would need re-validation.
- The "Enrolled" class is inherently ambiguous — it means the student's
  final outcome (Dropout vs. Graduate) simply hasn't happened yet, not that
  the model has genuinely identified a third *type* of student.
- The ADASYN and stacking comparisons ran on a 15,000-row subsample (for
  tractable notebook runtime) and a single train/validation split
  respectively — both conclusions are directional findings from this run,
  not guaranteed to hold at full data scale or across different random
  splits.
- No fairness/bias audit across demographic subgroups (e.g., nationality,
  gender) was performed here; a real deployment for an at-risk-student
  early-warning system would need one before use.
:::

## Conclusion

A moderate amount of feature engineering focused on *trajectory* rather than
snapshot performance — validated after the fact by SHAP, not just assumed
up front — combined with a standard gradient-boosted tree model, proper
cross-validation, and an honest evaluation of fancier techniques (ADASYN,
stacking) that turned out not to help here, is enough to build a
competitive, well-understood baseline for this task — while staying at a
scope appropriate for a teaching/portfolio project rather than a production
system.
